title: Present Active Verbs
objectives: understand the English verbal system and its parallels to Greek (tense, voice, mood, person, and number)
recognize and write the Present Active Indicative forms of Greek verbs
master 10 more high frequency vocabulary words
_objectives_note: Extracted verbatim from the TBK objectives field (0x8f7c7), DOSBox-confirmed in VERIFY-5D-RESPONSE2. Trailing commas dropped, matching the ch1/ch2 convention.

content.text: Verbs are words of action or state of being.

Zachary [[u]]drove[[/u]] the car.
Elliott [[u]]is[[/u]] a good kid.
We use verbs to make statements, give commands or express wishes.

[[u]]Come[[/u]] here.  [[g]]— command[[/g]]
Zach [[u]]may play[[/u]] basketball this year.  [[g]]— wish[[/g]]
(Mounce, pp. 116.; Wenham, p. 2; Summers, pp. 11ff)
Tense in English refers to the time of the action of the verb:

[[u]]Present:[[/u]]  Annette swims.
[[u]]Past:[[/u]]  Annette swam.
[[u]]Future:[[/u]]  Annette will swim.
In Greek, tense is used to refer not only to time, (when the event happened), but also to aspect (the type of action).
English has two voices to which Greek adds a third:

items.label: Active voice
items.text: subject does the action of the verb.

items.label: Passive voice
items.text: subject receives the action of the verb.

items.label: Middle voice
items.text: where the subject acts on him/herself (reflexive) or members of a group interact among themselves (reciprocal).  In Greek, self-interest may be reflected in the middle voice.

content.text:
Terry hit the ball.
Joy kissed Andy.

Terry was hit by the ball.
Joy was kissed by Andy.

Terry kicked himself.  [[g]]— reflexive[[/g]]
The players patted each other.  [[g]]— reciprocal[[/g]]

Middle verbs in Greek are usually (75% of the time) translated as an active or the middle changes the whole root meaning from the active form.  In this program, the middle will be translated active unless otherwise indicated.
(Mounce, p. 149; Summer, pp. 50-51)
Mood refers to the kind of reality of the action, or how the action of the verb is regarded.

items.label: Indicative mood
items.text: —simply states that something happened, e.g. Peter prays.

items.label: Imperative mood
items.text: —gives a command or exhortation, e.g.  Pray, Peter!

items.label: Subjunctive mood
items.text: —expresses a wish, possibility or potentiality, e.g.  Peter may pray.

content.text: There are 3 persons in Greek.

items.label: First person
items.text: is the person(s) speaking (I or we).

items.label: Second person
items.text: is the person(s) spoken to (you [singular or plural]).

items.label: Third person
items.text: is the person(s) or thing(s) spoken about (he, she, they, it).

content.text:
I studied Greek.
We studied Greek.

You studied Greek.
You both studied Greek.

She studied Greek.
They studied Greek.
Both English and Greek distinguish between singular (I, you, he, she, it) and the plural (we, you, they).
Verbs must agree with their subjects in both person and number.

He [[u]]hits[[/u]] the ball.
They [[u]]hit[[/u]] the ball.  (not "they hits the ball.")
(Mounce, p. 116)

The present active indicative will be our first verb paradigm.  It is the most frequently used "tense" in the New Testament (over 4000 times).  [[u]]Active[[/u]] means that the subject does the action of the verb as opposed to the middle or passive voices.  The [[u]]Indicative[[/u]] mood makes a statement as opposed to the Imperative or Subjunctive moods which we will study later.
Each form will be composed of a:
Stem + Pronominal ending — λύ + ω
content._note: Bold and indented in the original. λύ and ω are morpheme fragments with no standalone clips; rendered in ink, not tappable (Greek-tap exception).

content.text: The Present tense may denote either undefined (event simply happens) or continuous aspect (event was a process).
Thus it can be translated:

items.label: Continuous action
items.text: I am loosing, I am running

content.text: The context will determine which should be used.

Greek will often use the present tense to reference an event that actually happened in the past.  The historical present is used to add vividness to the narrative or, most often, it is an idiom.  It often occurs in narrative in the third person.  In these cases the present tense is simply translated by our past tense (e.g.  "he says" becomes "he said").
(Mounce, p. 115;  Machen, p. 20;  Summers, pp. 12)

endings.label: Endings
endings._note: Endings audio RESTORED (divergence log D-10): the original has a c_ending clip but the Endings button plays nothing (D15).

content.text: Sometimes a nu ( ν ) is added to the end of words ending in σι or ε, especially when it is followed by a word that begins with a vowel.  In English we do something similar with "a book" and "an item."  Thus sometimes the third plural form will be:
λύουσιν instead of λύουσι
(Machen, p. 27;  Summers, p. 13)

In English we make no distinction between a "you" singular and a "you" which is plural ("you all").  Some grammars use "thou" for the singular and "ye" for the plural.  Such usage is archaic and hence we will use "you" for both second person singular and plural.  You should be aware that in Greek a sharp distinction is made.
(Machen, p. 22)
Verbs are parsed or conjugated in the following format:
Tense, voice, mood, person, number, lexical root, English meaning

E.g.  λύω, present active indicative
1st person, singular from
λύω meaning "I loose, destroy."

items: Machen, J. Gresham.  New Testament Greek for Beginners (Toronto:  The Macmillan Company, 1923), pp. 20-22.
Mounce, William D.  Basics of Biblical Greek:  Grammar (Grand Rapids:  Zondervan, 1993), pp. 115-32.
Summers, Ray and Thomas Sawyer.  Essentials of New Testament Greek (Nashville:  Broadman & Holman, 1995), pp. 11-13.
Wenham, J. W.  The Elements of New Testament Greek (Cambridge:  Cambridge University Press, 1965), pp. 25-28.
